newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge says child porn law is constitutional.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge says child porn law is constitutional.

text.p: A federal judge ruled on Tuesday that a law outlawing computer-generated child pornography is constitutional.

U.S. District Judge Samuel Conti of San Francisco rejected arguments by opponents of the law that it was overbroad or "unconstitutionally vague" and said it did not constitute "an improper prior restraint on speech."

The Child Pornography Prevention Act of 1996 expanded the definition of child pornography, outlawing "any visual depiction" that "is, or appears to be, of a minor engaging in sexually explicit conduct."
Conti said the law was enacted specifically to combat the use of computer technology to produce pornography that conveys the impression that children were used in the photographs or images.

The Free Speech Coalition, a trade association representing the adult entertainment industry, joined several other people, including an artist whose paintings include large-scale nudes, in filing suit to challenge the constitutionality of the law.
The suit maintained that the law classified "visual depictions of adults who appear to be minors" as child pornography and said this violated the constitutional right to freedom of expression.
It said the law would ban "a wide array of sexually-explicit, non-obscene material that has serious literary, artistic, political and scientific value."
The suit was filed against Attorney General Janet Reno to halt enforcement of the law.

But Conti ruled in favour of Reno, saying in his written decision that the law provided a defence if the people depicted in the material were adults and the material was not presented as child pornography.

"The court finds that the Child Pornography Prevention Act is not overbroad. It specifies that only materials that do not use adults and that appear to be child pornography, even if they are digitally produced, are prohibited," Conti wrote.

"It is highly unlikely that the types of valuable works plaintiffs fear will be outlawed under the Child Pornography Prevention Act -- depictions used by the medical profession to treat adolescent disorders, adaptations of sexual works like 'Romeo and Juliet' and artistically-valued drawings and sketches of young adults engaging in passionate behaviour -- will be treated as 'criminal contraband'," he wrote.
